item.title: From Instantaneous Events to Musical Spans
item.author: sandy@sandymaguire.me (Sandy Maguire)
item.content:encoded:
We’ve been thinking a lot about musical structures over these last few posts. Today we’re going to look into some rhythmic concerns, and in particular, figure out how to turn a discrete signal of instantaneous events into something that actually looks like music.

Recall that we’ve been working with a Signal a type, which is a continuous function of Time -> a, packaged along with a set of “interesting times” that we might be interested in looking at. We smuggle discrete events into these interesting times. But what makes a time interesting?

One immediate answer, musically, is “when something happens.” That something could be a point in the meter, a chord change, the beginning of a note, the end of a note, a modulation, the return of a motif, every time an A is played, etc. Essentially, whenever you might think a time is interesting :)

Of these, we’re primarily going to focus on the beginning and end of notes today. Since once we’ve sorted that bit out, we have the better part of a musical MVP. It’s not going to be anywhere close to the vision, but it’s a necessary step along the path.

So what we’ve built so far is an Event type, which demarks instantaneous and momentary things. We have a Signal type which models things-over-time. It seems likely that in order to play notes we’re going to want a Signal of Events of something. Let’s say MIDI notes for now, since it’s an obvious sort of “computer music” interface.

The problem of course is that Events are instantaneous, but audible things are not; they necessarily have a duration. I played around with data structures in the style of interval trees for a long time before coming to the conclusion that that way lies folly.

Instead what seems to be the play is to explicitly model Spans:

data Span a = Span
  { duration :: Time
  , getSpan :: a
  }
  deriving stock (Eq, Ord, Show, Functor, Foldable, Traversable, Generic)

and then just generate them in our Signal. So rather than talk about Event MIDINote, we instead use Event (Span MIDINote). This is very much in the style of “regular old music scores” where there is explicit syntax for encoding the span of a note:

If you’re not familiar with music notation, the top line contains (after the funny “c” thing) the symbols for sounded notes. The first symbol takes up one unit of time, the next takes half that, and so on and so forth. The bottom line, in corresponding columns, are the same durations, except for silences rather than for sounded notes.

Anyway, the point here is namely that musicians are very much in the habit of thinking about “how long does this note sound for?” So attaching the Span to the note we want to play isn’t a very far-fetched idea at all.

That being said…

It turns out to be a drag to have to always be sticking durations on things. I suspect the pain is already internalized in some sort of Stockholm Syndrome, because every written notation and every computer program for music requires you to write down the damn durations.

As it happens, writing down the durations in advance is not very compositional. For example, if we stretch the time domain of our Signal (which is very reasonable and possible, since it’s just a function Time -> a), we’d expect the note durations to stretch too! But they can’t, since we’d have the type:

stretch :: Rational -> Signal a -> Signal a

which you’ll notice is polymorphic in a. Of course, we could do some ad-hoc bullshit where we stick in a typeclass constraint for “stretchable things” but this is the way of madness.

What if, instead, we were to derive the durations? After all, we already know when everything is, temporally-speaking. The first type that comes to mind for something like this would be:

SF (Event a)  (Event (Span a))

that is, a function over Signals, which takes an input stream of events and outputs a stream of events with a duration attached to them. What duration? Presumably until the next event! While this is a perfectly fine type (and isn’t very hard to implement), it has the obvious downside that it can’t represent silence. If a sound spans until the next sound, then there’s nowhere to stick any silence!

What I ended up with was to take two input event streams:

spanning :: SF (Event (), Event a) (Event (Span a))

where the Event () stream indicates changes and the Event a stream indicates beginnings of notes. Thus a note spans until the next Event a or Event () — whichever comes first.

The implementation is not very tricky. We use our primitive

ev2ev :: ([(Time, a)] -> [(Time, b)]) -> SF (Event a) (Event b)

and zip together the events with the tail of the events, taking the difference in their times. All that’s left is to combine the event streams, which is exactly what the Alternative instance on Event does:

spanning :: SF (Event (), Event a) (Event (Span a))
spanning = proc (end, a) -> do
  let merged = Just <$> a <|> Nothing <$ end
  ev2ev
    (\es -> catMaybes
      $ zipWith
          (\(t1, ema) (t2, _) -> case ema of
            Just a -> Just (t1, Span (t2 - t1) a)
            Nothing -> Nothing
          )
          es
      $ drop 1 es
    ) -< merged

I don’t know about you, but I think this is pretty cool. For two different reasons. The first is that we’ve accidentally just derived the notion of a musical voice, which is to say a logical grouping of musical events into something that could be sung by a person, or played on an instrument. Voices and (most) instruments only make one note at a time, which is exactly the postcondition of spanning.

The other cool thing here is that now we can change note lengths in the same way we can change chords and modulations — namely by doing transformations in SF. You can imagine a Signal Tension which describes how much tension the composer wants you to feel through the journey of the song. By deriving an event stream out of the modulating Tension, where events happen frequently in high tension situations, and less often under low tension, we can automatically drive note durations from our Tension parameter! I haven’t used a lot of DAWs, but my understanding is (and the clankers agree) that almost(?) no DAWs support duration as an automation. So we might be in terra nova over here!

Perhaps you’re starting to get a taste that maybe all of this “solving music” isn’t such a pipe dream after all. There’s clearly still a huge distance to travel before we’re anywhere close to anything useful, but the primitives do seem to be pulling their weight.

Of course, nobody wants to call spanning by hand, so next time we’ll see about finding nicer ways of generating horizontal structures.

item.title: Musical Signal Functions
item.author: sandy@sandymaguire.me (Sandy Maguire)
item.content:encoded:
We’ve been chatting for a few days about my vision for a constructive model of music. So far it’s been rather loosey-goosey; lots of vibes, some semantics, but nothing in the way of implementation. Today let’s get our boots muddy and do enough implementation that we have something concrete to talk about.

Events and Signals

In particular, in Musical Signals we discussed a Signal type that is a continuous function of time, equipped with a set of interesting times that we actually care about. In addition, we proposed an Event type that we will use in conjunction with Signals to signify sparse, discrete functions over time.

Let’s begin with Event. It’s just a little newtype wrapper around Maybe:

newtype Event a = MkEvent
  { eventToMaybe :: Maybe a
  }
  deriving stock (Foldable, Traversable, Generic)
  deriving newtype
    (Functor, Applicative, Monad, Eq, Ord, Show, Alternative, Semigroup, Monoid)

{-# COMPLETE Event, NoEvent #-}
pattern Event :: a -> Event a
pattern Event a = MkEvent (Just a)

pattern NoEvent :: Event a
pattern NoEvent = MkEvent Nothing

event :: b -> (a -> b) -> Event a -> b
event b f = maybe b f . eventToMaybe

As discussed in the footnote on that page, perhaps we want to not export the Event pattern, the MkEvent constructor, or the Applicative/Monad instances. That seems likely like the way to go, but I haven’t yet put much thought into whether it solves all the problems. So let’s export them for now (because they are genuinely useful!) and circle back at some point in the future.

My idea for implementing Signal is to keep around a bunch of continuous segments of function, each of which might have a time-of-interest at the exact instant that the segment starts. A Segment is defined thusly:

data Segment a = Segment
  { segVal :: Maybe a
  , segment :: Time -> a
    -- ^ Must be meaningfully defined for the *entirety* of time!
  }
  deriving stock Functor

The obvious Applicative Segment instance has the wrong semantics here, so we don’t provide it. The problem being that segVal corresponds to a value of the function at a time of interest. Which is to say, that if segVal is ever Just, it must remain Just as we ap our way through it! But Applicative isn’t powerful enough to do that, because filling in the missing data would require us to know what Time we should be sampling the function at.

We address the problem with a new combine function:

-- | Like 'liftA2' for 'Segment', when we have a concrete time to sample at.
combine :: Time -> (a -> b -> c) -> Segment a -> Segment b -> Segment c
combine t f (Segment a fa) (Segment b fb) =
  Segment
    ( asum
       [ liftA2 f a b
       , fmap (f (fa t)) b
       , fmap (flip f (fb t)) a
       ])
    (liftA2 f fa fb)

The asum here attempts to fill in the interesting value by combining the Maybes. If that fails, it then tries to fill it in by fmapping over either individual interesting value.

Collecting our Segments into a Signal requires a few helper functions: merge takes two sorted lists of pairs, and computes a sorted list of These. The idea being that if both lists have a key at the same index, we keep both of them around. If only one has a value, we tag it with which list it came from:

-- | Specialized 'Data.Align.align' for sorted pairs.
merge :: Ord a => [(a, b)] -> [(a, c)] -> [(a, These b c)]
merge [] ys       = fmap (fmap That) ys
merge (x : xs) [] = fmap (fmap This) (x : xs)
merge xx@((tx, x) : xs) yy@((ty, y) : ys) =
  case compare tx ty of
    LT -> (tx, This x) : merge xs yy
    GT -> (ty, That y) : merge xx ys
    EQ -> (tx, These x y) : merge xs ys

We use merge to define joining, which does a scanl of two sorted lists of Segments. The idea here is that the two lists are effectively interval trees, and the intervals are not guaranteed to line up. So we use a scanl hold onto the old value of each until it gets replaced with a new value.

joining
    :: Ord a
    => Segment b
    -> Segment c
    -> [(a, Segment b)]
    -> [(a, Segment c)]
    -> [(a, (Segment b, Segment c))]
joining a0 b0 as bs
  = drop 1
  $ scanl
    (\(_, (a, b)) (t, th) ->
      case th of
        This a'     -> (t, (a', open b))
        That b'     -> (t, (open a, b'))
        These a' b' -> (t, (a', b'))
    )
    ( error "unused initial time argument"
    , (a0, b0)
    )
  $ merge as bs

open :: Segment a -> Segment a
open s = s { segVal = Nothing }

With all that ceremony out of the way, we’re ready to define Signals, which contain an original Time -> a function with no interesting timepoints, and then a sorted list of new Segments.

-- | A piecewise function, built out of 'Segment' intervals.
data Signal a
  = Signal
      (Time -> a)
      -- ^ The function before we have switched to any 'Segment'.
      [(Time, Segment a)]
      -- ^ Sorted by time.
  deriving stock Functor

Of course, this is not the only possible implementation of Signal, nor am I claiming it’s the best one. It’s just one that I came up with that satisfied all the laws and wasn’t slower than molasses. I’ve also got a relatively-fresh new baby, so a lot of this got written on very little sleep. Anyway…

Despite Segment not admitting an Applicative instance, Signal does, because it keeps track of where each Segment begins.

instance Applicative Signal where
  pure a = Signal (pure a) mempty
  liftA2 f (Signal a as) (Signal b bs)
    = Signal (liftA2 f a b)
    $ fmap (uncurry $ \t -> (t,) . uncurry (combine t f))
    $ joining (Segment Nothing a) (Segment Nothing b) as bs

We can show that Signal preserves the semantics we gave by giving projections out of it into the semantic domain:

sample :: Signal a -> (Time -> a)
sample (Signal fa []) t = fa t
sample (Signal fa ((t0, sa) : as)) t =
  case compare t t0 of
    LT -> fa t
    EQ ->
      case sa of
        Segment Nothing f -> f t
        Segment (Just a) _ -> a
    GT -> sample (Signal (segment sa) as) t

This function is the continuous-μ given by our semantics. The discrete-μ is called values:

values :: Signal a -> [(Time, a)]
values (Signal _ as) = mapMaybe (traverse segVal) as

which returns a sorted list of interesting times (and their associated values.) In the Signal (Event a) case, we have a more useful function, which gets only those values which actually contain a discrete value:

events :: Signal (Event a) -> [(Time, a)]
events = mapMaybe (traverse eventToMaybe) . values

Arrows

Signals are nice representations of interesting-things-over-time. But the mental model of abstract modular synthesizers is not about interesting-things-over-time. It’s about ways of transforming and combining interesting-things-over-time.

Haskell has some deep-cut notation for this, namely the -XArrows extension and its related proc notation. Long-time readers of the blog will know that we’re no strangers to arrows here!

But as a very quick recap, given instances of Category and Arrow:

class Category a where
  id  :: a x x
  (.) :: a y z -> a x y -> a x z

class Category a => Arrow a where
  arr   :: (b -> c) -> a b c
  (***) :: a b c -> a b' c' -> a (b, b') (c, c')

we gain access to proc notation, which is very convenient for composing arrow values:

proc input ->
 a <- foo -< input
 b <- bar -< (input, a)
 let output = qux a b
 returnA -< output

This notation is syntactic sugar for the egregious:

  arr qux
. id *** bar
. arr (\i -> (snd i, i))
. id *** foo
. arr (\i -> (i, i))

which I think we can all agree is slightly less readable than the proc notation.

The rough vibes here is that Category a abstracts the notion of what a function is. Rather than using Haskell -> arrows, we can instead use a-arrows. The Category methods (.) and id do exactly what you’d expect — composition and identity of a-arrows.

The Arrow a class extends this with some way of turning arbitrary Haskell arrows into a-arrows, as well as a way to run two different a-arrows on the fst and snd of a (Haskell) product type. The exact semantics of what that looks like depends on your a-arrow type (much like the exact semantics of do notation depend on your choice of a monad!)

Anyway, to pull back to musical transformations. If we were to find some sort of music-aware Arrow instance, proc-notation is exactly what we’d want in order to “run patches” in our abstract modular synthesizer. That is to say, it provides the plumbing for moving music in and out of transformations. As a teaser for what’s to come, here’s a little example from my sandbox:

-- A horizontal pattern describing an unfolding dyadic voice-leading that
-- descends by fifth, before swapping the voices by moving away from one
-- another.
divergence = replicateH 12 $ foldMap dnote
  [ voiceLead 0 3
  , expand 0 1
  ]

song = horizontal $ resize 0.25 $ proc i -> do
  -- Compute an abstract voice leading over time
  vl <- liftH msumE <<< divergence -< i

  -- Apply that voice leading to the first two notes of a triad
  ns <- replicateH 12 $ with id -< applyVoiceLeading vl $ chord triad
  returnA -< ns

which describes this this nice little dyad expansion:

If we replace the last line with:

  -- Convert the "polyphony" into "counterpoint"
  let (lo :> hi :> Nil) = toV ns

  -- Clamp the lo voice so it stays within its register
  lo' <- liftH $ clampOctave (-9, 0) 0.5 -< lo

  -- Convert the "counterpoint" back into "polyphony"
  returnA -< fromV $ lo' :> hi :> Nil

we get this:

and of course we can also clamp the upper voice:

  -- Clamp the voices so they stay within their registers
  lo' <- liftH $ clampOctave (-9, 0) 0.5 -< lo
  hi' <- liftH $ clampOctave (0, 7) 0.5 -< hi

  -- Convert the "counterpoint" back into "polyphony"
  returnA -< fromV $ lo' :> hi' :> Nil

and we get this:

Now I’ll be the first to admit that this is a completely unusable DSL. But it does actually work! And if you squint, you can sort of see the modular synthesizer idea at play. Inside the proc notation, we are sampling all of our Signals simultaneously, but routing the output of (eg) the voice leading into the input of replicateH $ with id, which is what builds out the rhythmic pattern. Then we take the output of that, separate it into Signals of its constituent voices, and feed those into clampOctave, which moves a Signal’s notes into the given range of scale degrees.

Something cool but not pictured here, clampOctave takes a second argument (the 0.5) which tells it to look into the future and not perform any displacement if it would need to move again within that 0.5 of a measure. This is some sort of “retro-hysteresis” where signals can depend on their future values! Which sounds crazy when you’re thinking about wiring up synthesizers, but much less crazy when you’re sitting down writing out a score. Of course the notes in your score can depend on notes that happen later on in the song! One of the many benefits of explicitly modeling time in Signals.

Signal Functions

Hopefully you’re excited to see how we go about doing any of this acausal wizardry stuff. But it all starts from getting proc notation working. Which, recall, means we need a type to give an Arrow instance to.

Behold, the signal function (SF):

newtype SF a b = SF
  { runSF :: Signal a -> Signal b
  }
  deriving (Functor, Applicative) via WrappedArrow SF a
  deriving (Semigroup, Monoid) via Ap (SF a) b

which you will note is literally a function between Signals. Its Category instance comes immediately from Haskell functions’ instance:

instance Category SF where
  id = SF id
  SF g . SF f = SF (g . f)

The Arrow instance is similarly straightforward — separate out the product, run the functions on each half, then use the applicative instance to combine them back into a single Signal:

instance Arrow SF where
  arr = SF . fmap
  SF f *** SF g = SF $ \sg ->
    liftA2 (,) (f $ fmap fst sg) (g $ fmap snd sg)

That’s really all there is to it! We can give some means of introducing SFs:

constS :: Signal a -> SF x a
constS = SF . const

as well as a few primitives whose definition we don’t have time to get into:

-- | Create a single occurrence of an Event at the given time.
at :: Time -> a -> SF x (Event a)

-- | Convert a discrete stream into a continuous one, by holding the value of
-- the last event seen.
hold :: a -> SF (Event a) a

-- | Like 'hold', but backwards in time. Hold the value of the /next/ event that
-- will occur.
fhold :: a -> SF (Event a) a

-- | Stateful folds over Events
scanE :: (s -> a -> (s, b)) -> s -> SF (Event a) (Event b)

-- | Full-scale rewrites of Event streams
ev2ev :: ([(Time, a)] -> [(Time, b)]) -> SF (Event a) (Event b)

-- | Run the first SF until the 'Event' occurs, then switch into the
-- continuation.
switch :: SF a (b, Event c) -> (c -> SF a b) -> SF a b

(for completeness’ sake, there ought to be time-reverse versions of scanE and switch too!)

This seems like a good place to leave it for now. In the next post we’ll discuss how to turn all of this abstract machinery into something that actually resembles music.

item.title: What Composing Music Could Look Like
item.author: sandy@sandymaguire.me (Sandy Maguire)
item.content:encoded:
In the last post, we discussed the algebraic structure of horizontal structures. But I realized I haven’t actually communicated the argument behind why we might care about that algebraic structure. So rather than diving directly into the technical stuff I had planned for today, let’s hash that out first.

If you recall, where we ended up was an abstract type Signal a which I claim is a precursor to horizontal musical structures, with the following common algebras:

type Signal a
instance Functor Signal
instance Applicative Signal
instance Foldable Signal
instance Semigroup a => Semigroup (Signal a)
instance Semigroup a => Monoid (Signal a)

It’s worth considering what each of these ideas means, musically. And once we’ve sorted that out, it’s worth thinking about what other musical structure we might want on top.

We can think about a Signal a as being a continuous function of as over time, combined with a set of times that we’re actually interested in. So what exactly does that mean? The continuous function part is just there to fill in the details when we change our minds about what times we want to look at.

With our Functor instance, we can do per-note (or per-whatever is held in the horizontal structure) transformations. For example, fmap (+ 1) transforms

into

But it also does more interesting things; fmap (!! 1) (where !! n selects voice n) transforms

into

Furthermore, nobody says the a in Signal a need be something that is musically meaningful. A Signal is just a function from time to something; so we could do something crazy like building a Signal DayName that is a week-long signal moving from Monday to Sunday at a rate of one a day. We could then use the Functor instance to transform these labels into something more musically meaningful — perhaps into motifs or numbers of repeats, or something like that.

Our Semigroup instance gives us a <> operation, which combines things that happen at the same time. What it means to “combine things” depends on the things being combined. But as a little vibe check, we can use <> to smush together two little motifs:

into

This example one is very vibes, so don’t read TOO much into it. The important part is that “things that happen at the same time get smushed together.” We’ll discuss in MUCH MORE DETAIL sometime in the future what sorts of smushing might be musically meaningful.

The Applicative structure is very similar to the Semigroup, except that instead of smushing things together, we can run a function that depends on the values in both things. This one is unfortunately impossible to show in standard musical notation, and wiring up some custom visualization isn’t a good use of my nanowrimo time.

But let’s use our IMAGINATION instead. Imagine a voice-leading that looks like this (realized over a C-major triad):

We can use our applicative instance to retarget the voice leading over any other chord. For example, given this one:

Invoking liftA2 applyVoiceLeading over these two musical pieces gives us this remarkable chord progression:

If you’re familiar with lots of harmony, you can see that both progressions are structurally equivalent — a neo-Riemannian P transform, followed by an efficient voice leading from CM to E#M, followed by the outer two voices switching pitch classes by moving in opposite directions.1

Of course, nothing requires us to use the same chord throughout. We can apply our same voice leading pattern to a series of changing chords, for example:

which results in

You’ll notice we’re getting very interesting results without doing much work at all. I picked some random voice leadings and some random chords, and the computer did all of the work of figuring out what notes I’m gesturing at.

Some other things you could do with this: instead of voice leadings, put scalar modulations. Or note durations! Or put voice numberings and project chords down to individual voices (which is different than the functor case, because here we can change which voice gets to sound.) Better yet, do all of the above, continuously, at different time scales.

What I think this ends up looking like in practice is something akin to a modular synthesizer. You can plug the outputs of different signals into the inputs of others. But unlike any modular synthesizer you’ve ever played with, here our signals are allowed to carry macroharmonies, voice leadings, modulations, tension, motifs, rhythm, registral expansion, dynamics, timbre, or even just arbitrary mathematical functions.

That’s probably enough for now. In the next post we’ll actually get around to looking at the implementation of Signal and then giving better composable semantics around it.

  1. I extracted all the moves here from Tymoczko’s masterpiece Tonality: An Owner’s Manual.↩︎

item.title: Musical Signals
item.author: sandy@sandymaguire.me (Sandy Maguire)
item.content:encoded:
The last blog post served as an overview of my music project — what it is, why it is, and roughly what success will look like. Today we’ll get into some of the nitty gritty details that will help put the project onto a firm footing.

In order to have any chance of not confusing ourselves, we must first be precise about what exactly it is we’re talking about. That means we’ll have to model out some types, and, importantly what those types mean. Recall that one of our desiderata is that whatever it is we’re building must be capable of expressing any music from any culture from any time period, including those times and cultures which do not yet exist.

The trick then is to make a series of extensible types, each one providing some aspect of functionality, and letting people compose them together for themselves. Future users can add their own types with their own functionality, and reuse as much of the system that is meaningful to reuse.

By my reckoning, music is made up of some combination of the following:

  1. some notion of time, generally considered to be rhythmic content, or “horizontal structures.”
  2. some notion of simultaneity, generally considered to be chords, polyphony, or “vertical structures.”
  3. things that can happen, generally considered to be musical content of some sort. Perhaps this is pitches (as in musical scores), or waveforms (as in musical playback.)

As a placeholder to get our bearings, let’s imagine the first two elements as types:

type Horizontal a
type Vertical a

and postulate both a Pitch and Waveform type for item three:

type Pitch
type Waveform

By composing these types in different ways, different ideas of music fall out. Several examples:

  1. Horizontal () describes purely time-based structures; eg. rhythmic ideas
  2. Horizontal Pitch is a simple tune, the sort you can whistle
  3. Vertical Pitch is a single chord.
  4. Horizontal (Vertical Pitch) is what you get at a campfire from someone who only knows how to play chords on the guitar. In the jargon, this is “polyphonic” music.
  5. Vertical (Horizontal Pitch) is multiple independent tunes happening simultaneously. In the jargon, this is “contrapuntal” music.
  6. Vertical (Horizontal Waveform) is what you get in a DAW — independent tracks, each of which lets you move recorded samples along its own timeline.

Of course, this is all vibes right now, since we haven’t discussed what exactly any of these types actually are. But this should be enough to wet your whistle; if we can deliver types that match these vibes, we clearly have an amazing starting point.

As a point of note, this first step is where I went wrong in my last public attempt. There I postulated that all music is what here would be described as Vertical (Horizontal a). And I gave unsatisfying answers for what Vertical and Horizontal are, to boot!

Shame. Sorrow.

Anyway. Let’s leave Vertical alone for now, and focus our attention on Horizontal, since it seems to be the crux of the interesting stuff here. However, rather than using up the musically-relevant name Horizontal, let’s go with Signal, since we’re going to be building up this idea in several pieces.

By our vibes, a Signal is a time-based structure. Which is to say, it ought to describe two things: 1) what happens, and 2) when it happens. That’s a pretty big constraint on the search space; the only other question is whether it ought to be continuous or discrete. In the continuous case, we have:

μ (Signal a) = Time -> a

and in the discrete:

μ (Signal a) = [(Time, a)]  -- ordered by monotonically ascending Time

where μ should be read as “the meaning of.” That is to say, we’re trying to pin down the semantics of Signal without saying anything about how we’re actually going to implement this thing.

This is my first point of confusion. Composition (in the programming sense) is significantly better with the Time -> a denotation, but when I listen to music I “hear” it “discretely.” I think. Maybe. Like I said, I am confused.

Rather than choose between these two options, I am cheating and choosing BOTH. HA HA HA. This is intellectually dishonest, but it’s a decision that needs to be made early on, and making progress seems to be dependent on choosing something. Hopefully when everything has clarified down the road, we can return to this decision and make a better choice.

Sorry, let me back up. What the hell am I talking about? I have the advantage of knowing where I’m going, so I imagine it’s pretty disjointed without that. Concretely, I am torn between a few things:

  1. The discrete choice vibes better with my classical piano training, where “music” is rendered as a score with discrete symbols on a page
  2. I have a strong bias towards being able to generate these symbols on a page with this system I’m making
  3. But the discrete choice doesn’t admit nearly as much algebraic structure. For example, it seems very desirable to have an applicative structure on Signal. The usual list applicative is seems musically meaningless (taking the cartesian product of all the notes in a piece? yeah ok). What seems more likely is a pointwise “zippy” applicative. But in a discrete framing, there isn’t enough data to combine two Signal structures that are out of phase with one another.

So, the unsatisfying solution here is to just do both. Rather than picking between a discrete and a continuous representation, just keep both around:

μ (Signal a) = (Time -> a, Set Time)

That is, represent the Signal structure as a continuous function out of time, but also keep track of a set of interesting times!

We get quite a lot of nice algebraic structure on top of this thing:

μ (Signal a) = (Time -> a, Set Time)

instance Functor Signal where
  μ (fmap f a) = first (fmap f) (μ a)

instance Applicative Signal where
  μ (pure a) = (const a, mempty)
  μ (liftA2 f a b) = (liftA2 f *** (<>)) (μ a) (μ b)

instance Semigroup a => Semigroup (Signal a) where
  μ (a <> b) = μ a <> μ b

instance Monoid a => Monoid (Signal a) where
  μ mempty = mempty

instance Foldable Signal where
  μ (foldMap f a) = uncurry foldMap (μ a)

which I always take as a sign that I’m on the right track.

Armed with Signal, we can give some rudimentary combinators on it. For example, we can lift functions:

lift :: (Time -> a) -> Signal a
μ (lift f) = (f, mempty)

and we can generate stepwise signals:

stepwise :: a -> [(Time, a)] -> Signal a
μ (stepwise a0 []) = pure a0
μ (stepwise a0 ((t0, a) : as)) = \t ->
  case t < t0 of
    True -> a0
    False -> μ (stepwise a as)

Attentive readers will notice that nothing yet ever actually introduces any times-of-interest into a Signal. Here is where my earlier belly-aching comes back to bite. I’d LIKE VERY MUCH to be able to say “discrete Signals have a different type than continuous ones.” So maybe we add an Event type:

μ (Event a) = Maybe a

and then say we can make discrete signals:

discrete :: [(Time, a)] -> Signal (Event a)
μ (discrete as) = (\t -> lookup t as, Set.fromList $ fmap fst as)

with the implicit promise that if you have a Signal (Event a) then it must be a discrete Signal! Unfortunately, this is not the sort of promise we can keep; it’s trivial to construct a densely packed Signal of Events:

notActuallyDiscrete :: Signal a -> Signal (Event a)
μ notActuallyDiscrete = fmap Just . μ

Alas. Shame. Sorrow.

Nevertheless, we are just going to ignore this issue, and pretend like any Signal (Event a) must be discrete and sparse! I am eminently aware of how disappointed Conal would be by my motivated reasoning here. I’m disappointed in myself! Unfortunately I don’t have a better answer other than to split up the continuous and discrete cases, but that throws away a bunch of the compositionality that I want. I am confident there is a better solution here but damned if I know what it is.1

Anyway, I’m writing this in the darkness at 5am before my family awakens, but I hear stirring so it’s probably time to stop. If you have any lovely ideas about how to solve this discrete/continuous discrepancy, I’d love to hear them.

Next we’ll look at signal functions, and give to-my-knowledge a novel application of Arrows for music.

  1. One titillating idea is to simply not expose any introductory forms for Event. I haven’t explored this much, since it would mean we don’t get an applicative functor over Event. Thinking about it now, it’d still be fine to expose the Nothing-analogous constructor, so we could still give mempty. And perhaps this is the first motivating case I’ve ever found for giving only a Apply instance instead of a full Applicative.↩︎

item.title: An Overview of an Ambitious Music Project
item.author: sandy@sandymaguire.me (Sandy Maguire)
item.content:encoded:
It’s November. And you know what that means. National Novel Writing Month. Rather than writing a novel, I thought it’d be fun to do something like in 2016 when I wrote my first textbook. But this time around, I’m going to bash out all of the ideas about a constructive theory of music that have been banging around in my head for a few years.

Many years ago, I read Composing Contracts: an adventure in financial engineering, in which Haskell King Simon Peyton Jones descends unwittingly into the world of financial instruments. And being a “red-blooded functional programmer,” he designs a bunch of combinators which model the entire complexity of dozens of financial instruments, as well as an infinitely many that nobody had ever thought to ask for.

This paper has always been wildly inspirational to me, and alongside Compiling to Categories, is the clearest example of the power of pure, strongly-typed, functional programming, and its ability to model the wider, messier world.

So, wanting to learn how to flex these muscles for myself, I set off many years ago on a quest to try to tackle the hardest problem I could think of, that I felt like I had any chance whatsoever of succeeding at — music. After all, “so much of life’s failure consists in holding yourself to too low a standard.”

The goal is, and has always been, to develop something equivalent to Brent Yorgey’s amazing diagrams library. Diagrams is a combinator library in Haskell which abstracts away the “how” of drawing a picture from the “what picture do you want to draw?” For example, here’s how you draw a Sierpinski triangle:

sierpinski 1 = triangle 1
sierpinski n =     s
                 ===
              (s ||| s) # centerX
  where s = sierpinski (n-1)

which you might notice is exactly the obvious definition of what a Sierpinski triangle is — recursive copies of itself arranged in a triangle.

So the question I’ve been chasing for years is “what is an equivalently elegant approach to composing music?” I spent a good chunk of my holiday season last year struggling to find a good starting point here. With the benefit of hindsight, and of being a year older and wiser, I’ve made a great deal of progress since then.

But before diving into exactly what that progress means, I think it’s worth discussing what explicitly the goals here are (and what they are not.) Some desiderata:

  1. The system must be capable of expressing any music, from any culture, from any time (this includes music and styles that do not yet exist.)
  2. It must be easy to get good results out of the system.
  3. Understanding the system should teach you something about music.

These three desiderata are an extreme set of constraints on the solution space. Desideratum 1 means that we can’t take anything for granted. For example, we cannot assume that there are 12 pitch classes, since this would immediately eliminate microtonal music. Nor can we privilege harmonic function, since this isn’t an idea that seems to be shared by non-Western traditional music.

Desideratum 2 means that we can’t be happy with only a mathematical model. Yes, to a first approximation, set theory can describe anything, but lots of things are pretty egregious to articulate in set theory! This gives rise to the need for musically-meaningful combinators. I think the [kaleidoscope diagram] is a striking visual example of this idea. It’s a piece of code that given any image whatsoever can produce a new image which is a kaleidoscope of that thing. With a little hand waving here, you can imagine a set of musical combinators which approach a given motif, which ramp up the tension, which introduce syncopation, which produce senses of resolution. This also means we must put a great deal of thought into how musical ideas are represented, and how they can be combined.

Desideratum 3 means we can’t just hand the problem off to some LLM or some other probabilistic mechanism.

Under these constraints, it’s immediately evident that almost no existing music theory is up to the task. As best I can tell, the field of music theory is primarily focused on analysis of existing music rather than on general techniques for creating new music. Perhaps an argument can be made that you must be able to spot greatness in order to produce it for yourself, but this is relatively unconvincing to me. Attempting to perform post-hoc analysis of music without a constructive theory seems analogous to decompiling computer code without a language to decompile it into. At best you might find some statistical patterns (V chords often go to I), but this doesn’t seem like it ought to lend itself much to actually writing good music. Will it out-compete a Markov chain trained on the same probabilities?

The best we can do with most existing music theory is (to the extent that it is constructive [which is extremely few and far between]) relegate it to combinator status. A grammar of functional harmony can exist as a DSL on top of the core music structures. Voice leading spaces ala Tymoczko1 can be expressed by their own notions of pitch, alongside operations and elimination forms.

So that’s the overview. All in all, it’s a very ambitious project. I am not interested in hearing from you if you think this cannot be done. If you’re right, I’ll end up with egg on my face, but that’s my problem. However, if this is the sort of thing that piques your interest as much as it has mine, please do get in touch.

In the next post we’ll discuss the denotative elements of music.

  1. Dmitri Tymoczko has the distinction of being the only music theorist I’ve found who is precise enough to be more than not even wrong. Rather amazingly, he also seems to be right! Coincidence?↩︎

item.title: Reviewing Again
item.author: sandy@sandymaguire.me (Sandy Maguire)
item.content:encoded:
Last time, we took a stroll down memory lane to review some ancient code I wrote, and see what/how I’d do things differently now. That was fun, and I have a new banger for us today.

Today’s example comes from the same place — a little vim-like text editor I was working on. Vim has this “repeat” operator which just does the same thing you did last time. It’s nice. Delete a word. Running repeat deletes another word. Kinda dinky in this example, but it can also rerun “increment every number in the next four paragraphs.”

Anyway, so that’s the feature I was trying to duplicate. But the action I was running might have done some IO, and I didn’t want to repeat the IO (because maybe the IO was to gather some input from the user, and repeating shouldn’t ask again.)

I was still high on my own supply of writing monads, so I approached this problem with a custom monad. The gist of the API was:

-- | A monad transformer adding the ability to record the results of IO actions
-- and later replay them.
data Again m a
instance Monad m => Monad (Again m)
instance MonadIO m => MonadIO (Again m)
instance MonadTrans Again

-- | Runs an action and records all of its sampled IO. Returns a action which
-- when invoked will use the recorded IO.
runAgain
    :: Monad m
    => Again m a
    -> m (m a)

-- | Marks an IO action to be memoized after its first invocation.
again
    :: ( MonadIO m
       , Typeable r
       )
    => IO r
    -> Again m r

I’m actually pretty impressed with past-me on this one. That’s a clean API, and the implementation was pretty cute.

newtype Again m a = Again
  { runAgain' :: RWST () [Dynamic] [Dynamic] m a
  }

once
    :: forall m r
     . ( MonadIO m
       , Typeable r
)
    => IO r
    -> Again m r
once action = do
    a <- dequeue >>= \case
        Just x  -> return . fromJust $ fromDynamic x
        Nothing -> liftIO action
    tell [toDyn a]
    return a
  where
    dequeue :: MonadState [r] m => m (Maybe r)
    dequeue = do
        get >>= \case
            []     -> return Nothing
            (x:xs) -> do
                put xs
                return $ Just x

The trick here is to keep MonadState [Dynamic] and a MonadWriter [Dynamic] instances around. This code uses the MonadState to pop off IO actions it’s already run, and the MonadWriter to keep track of new IO actions it needs to cache. The “magic” happens in runAgain, which runs it through once with an empty state, and then returns a new action with the MonadWriter results moved into the state for the next time around:

runAgain
    :: Monad m
    => Again m a
    -> m (m a)
runAgain action = do
    (a, w) <- evalRWST (runAgain' action) () []
    return $ do
        evalRWST (runAgain' action) () w
        return a

Simple. Clean. Elegant. Too bad it doesn’t actually work.

The following program crashes with an error coming from the unsafe use of fromJust in once:

oops :: Again (StateT Bool IO) ()
oops =
  -- Branch on the StateT
  lift get >>= \case
    -- The first time around...
    False -> do
      -- Cache a unit value
      once $ print ()
      -- Change the state value
      lift $ put True

    -- Since the state changed at the end of the first branch, we will take this
    -- branch the second time around...
    True -> do
      -- Calling 'once' the second time around gets its value from the cache,
      -- which has type @()@. But at this callsite, it ought to have type
      -- @Bool -> Bool@. Uh oh!
      f <- once $ pure not
      lift $ print ("uh oh!", f True)


ohNo :: IO ((), Bool)
ohNo = flip runStateT False $ do
  m <- runAgain oops
  m

The attack here comes from the fact that we can force the Again program down a different code path its second time around. And that second time, it encounters a call to once which has a different type than the one it cached. Thus, trying to reuse the cache leads to what is effectively a type error at runtime.

What actually went wrong here? The problem is that monads are too powerful. Since the only way to compose monads is via bind (m a -> (a -> m b) -> m b), we are forced to extend a monadic value of type m a by a function of type a -> m b. Which is to say that the “next thing to do” in a monadic computation is always going to be a function. And functions are completely opaque. So, once we’re given a monad, there’s simply no way to know what it’s going to do without actually running the continuation.

The problem arises from the fact that that continuation can invisibly branch. My Again monad was attempting to statically analyze the monadic computation, and cache the IO results in a queue. But as oops shows, it’s trivial to break this sort of static analysis. Because the branch is hidden inside of a function, and there’s no way to determine which branches a function didn’t take.

But I didn’t know that eleven years ago, so I give myself a pass on this one. Nevertheless, let’s tackle this problem with the wisdom of ages.

No More Monads

So if the problem with my previous implementation of Again is that it’s a monad, what options do we have? As it happens, there are two very nice options available to us here: arrows and selective applicative functors. We’ll discuss arrows for now, and come back to selectives.

Long time readers might remember a series on arrows from a few years back. But if you don’t, that’s OK; you’re still welcome here. A quick recap:

Arrows are a generalization of functions. Like functions, they take two type parameters (an input and an output). Like functions, they come with an identity arrow. They compose “end to end” just like functions do. These three properties are expressed as a Category superclass, which we usually call c and write infix:

class Category (c :: Type -> Type -> Type) where
  id  :: x `c` x
  (.) :: (y `c` z) -> (x `c` y) -> (x `c` z)

In addition to being categories, arrows also come with a means of transforming regular functions into arrows, and of mapping arrows over pairs:

class Category c => Arrow c where
  arr :: (x -> y) -> (x `c` y)
  (***) :: (x `c` x') -> (y `c` y') -> ((x, y) `c` (x', y'))

What’s neat about arrows is that their values are function-like things, rather than being actually functions. That means when we compose arrows, we compose values whose internals we get to choose. Which in turn, means that static analysis is possible again!

Attentive readers will notice that there isn’t actually any way for arrows-as-such to be able to branch. To gain that capability, they require an additional ArrowChoice, which equips them with the ability to lift arrows over Either:

class Arrow c => ArrowChoice c where
  (+++) :: (x `c` x') -> (y `c` y') -> (Either x y `c` Either x' y')

To wet our whistle, let’s write a little helper Arrow that shows that the composition of an applicative functor with an arrow is itself an arrow:

newtype Static m c x y = Static
  { unStatic :: m (c x y)
  }

The arrow instances for (Applicative m, Arrow c) => Static m c are the usual trick of using applicative functions to lift operations into the right place. For example, identity is just pure id, and composition isliftA2` of composition:

instance (Category c, Applicative m) => Category (Static m c) where
  id = Static $ pure id
  Static g . Static f = Static $ liftA2 (.) g f

We can do the same trick for arr and (***):

instance (Arrow c, Applicative m) => Arrow (Static m c) where
  arr = Static . pure . arr
  Static f *** Static g = Static $ liftA2 (***) f g

as well as for (+++):

instance (ArrowChoice c, Applicative m) => ArrowChoice (Static m c) where
  Static f +++ Static g = Static $ liftA2 (+++) f g

What’s nice about this Static construct we’ve built is that it gives us two degrees of freedom. We’re free to choose an arrow whose structure we’re going to reuse, and an underlying applicative functor (which can give us “static” effects as we’re building the underlying arrow.)

The idea here is that we can put the cache-building machinery inside of the applicative functor, but the cache-reading machinery inside of the underlying arrow.

Constructing Again, Again

It’s worth knowing about the Kleisli arrow:

newtype Kleisli m a b = Kleisli
  { runKleisli :: a -> m b
  }

instance Monad m => Category (Kleisli m)
instance Monad m => Arrow (Kleisli m)
instance Monad m => ArrowChoice (Kleisli m)

which says that any monadic bind function is itself an arrow. Implementing the instances yourself is a fun exercise if you’re new to this stuff. We can reuse Kleisli as our underlying arrow, which when you expand everything out, we get:

newtype Again m a b = Again
  { unAgain :: Static m (Kleisli m) a b
  }
  deriving newtype (Category, Arrow, ArrowChoice)

runAgain :: Monad m => Again m a b -> m (a -> m b)
runAgain = fmap runKleisli . unStatic . unAgain

What I think is particularly cool about this is that runAgain is just the composition of the newtype unwrappers, and yet its type is extremely reminiscent of my ten-year-ago implementation:

runAgain  -- the original
    :: Monad m
    => Again m a
    -> m (m a)

This is an instance of a more general principle, which is that the final “observation” you want to make of your type is always a good representation of that type. It’s not the only representation, but it’s always a reasonable choice. Appropriately enough, this is known as a final encoding.

Anyway. How can we implement once? By way of onceF:

onceF :: (MonadIO m, Ord a) => (a -> IO b) -> Again m a b
onceF m = Again $ Static $ do
  cache <- liftIO $ newIORef mempty
  pure $ Kleisli $ \a -> liftIO $ do
    cacheMap <- readIORef cache
    case M.lookup a cacheMap of
      Just b -> pure b
      Nothing -> do
        b <- m a
        modifyIORef' cache $ M.insert a b
        pure b

once :: MonadIO m => IO b -> Again m a b
once m = arr (const ()) >>> onceF (const m)

onceF works by constructing a cache :: IORef (Map a b) at the Static level. Each call to onceF gets a unique cache. Then we drop into the implementation of the Kleisli arrow (which recall happens at runtime.) Inside the Kleisli, we check to see if the map has a value at the requested a, and if so, return the cached b. If not, we run our function and cache it.

Since there’s no Dynamic tomfoolery here that is existentializing away our types, we don’t need to worry about the oops attack; Haskell’s type system guarantees we can’t construct such a thing.

Because Again isn’t a Monad, it can’t be a MonadIO either. But it’s nice to be able to provide the equivalent of liftIO:

againF :: MonadIO m => (a -> IO b) -> Again m a b
againF = Again . Static . pure . Kleisli . fmap liftIO

again :: MonadIO m => IO a -> Again m x a
again m = arr (const ()) >>> againF (const m)

So that completes our arrow-based implementation of Again. But there’s still something left undone.

Circling Back to Selectives

I said earlier that selective applicative functors would be an alternative approach to implementing Again. Selectives rightfully sit between Applicative and Monad in the functor hierarchy, but were discovered too late, and everyone was still kind of annoyed about having had just stuck Applicative into the hierarchy.

What, precisely is a selective functor? It’s a different solution to the problem of “monads are too powerful” which gives us a branching primitive to play with. Behold:

class Applicative f => Selective f where
  select :: f (Either a b) -> f (a -> b) -> f b

select says that you might have an a, in which case you must run the provided f (a -> b). But maybe you have a b, in which case you may run the effects of the f (a -> b). But nobody’s forcing you to.

Since there are still no raw function continuations to be seen here, we can use select to provide branching to our programs. But all of the branches can be identified statically, since we’re only operating on f values, again, whose internals we can control.

In fact, by aggressively nesting select calls, you can get back a version of monadic bind — so long as you have a finite number of select calls you’d need to make:

bindS
    :: (Selective f, Enum a, Bounded a, Eq a)
    => f a
    -> (a -> f b)
    -> f b

(the implementation of which is fun if you’re looking for a challenge)

Anyway, all of this is to say that we could have equally structured our Again as a selective functor rather than as an arrow! But ArrowChoice is at least as powerful as Selective, so given all of our hard work already, we can pull out a Selective instance for free.

What do I mean when I say “at least as powerful?” It means we can derive it for free, given an ArrowChoice instance. Behold, the GenericArrow newtype, which exists only for us to have something to attach some instances to.

newtype GenericArrow c x a = GenericArrow
  { unGenericArrow :: c x a
  }
  deriving newtype (Category, Arrow, ArrowChoice)

Here we use newtype deriving to say that if c is a category/arrow/arrowchoice, then GenericArrow c is too. But now we can show that having Arrow is enough to get Functor and Applicative instance:

instance Arrow c => Functor (GenericArrow c x) where
  fmap f c = arr f . c

instance Arrow c => Applicative (GenericArrow c x) where
  pure = arr . const
  liftA2 f x y = (x &&& y) >>> arr (uncurry f)

Then, given an ArrowChoice, we can get an implementation of select:

instance ArrowChoice c => Selective (GenericArrow c x) where
  select te tk = proc b -> do
    e <- te -< b
    case e of
      Left x -> do
        k <- tk -< b
        returnA -< k x
      Right y -> returnA -< y

Here we don’t have the option of choosing to invoke tk in the Right case. But that’s OK, because in Again, doing so would correspond to creating caches for branches that don’t need it.

Given all of this, we can now derive Functor up to Selective for Again:

newtype Again m a b = Again
  { unAgain :: Static m (Kleisli m) a b
  }
  deriving newtype (Category, Arrow, ArrowChoice)
  deriving (Functor, Applicative, Selective) via GenericArrow (Again m) a

which means that users can now choose between the arrow hierarchy and the functor hierarchy for how they’d like to think about building Again actions. And to nudge them even a little further, we can introduce something that looks like a monad transformer, removing the input parameter:

type AgainT m = Again m ()

runAgainT :: Monad m => AgainT m a -> m (m a)
runAgainT = fmap ($ ()) . runAgain

Clean. Tidy. Actually works this time around.

item.title: Code-Reviewing My First Monad Implementation
item.author: sandy@sandymaguire.me (Sandy Maguire)
item.content:encoded:
I’ve been wanting to get back into the habit of blogging, and thought a fun project would be to go back through my old code and review it as the programmer I am now. So let’s do that.

Eleven years ago, I was so proud to written my first monad that I typed up a big olblog post about it. This seems like a fun thing to revisit, so let’s do it.

To save you the trouble of reading that ancient-ass blog post, here’s the gist. Given a big piece of state, that has many smaller stateful subcomponents, for example, a World is full of Buffers:

data World = World
  { wBuffers :: [Buffer]
  , wCurrent :: Int
  , wMode    :: Mode
  }

data Buffer = Buffer
  { bFilename :: FilePath
  , bContent  :: String
  }

my monad acted like StateT except that you can restrict the piece of the state you’re allowed to manipulate without losing the ability to look at the rest of the state.

In the blog post, this monad is called Jurisdiction, but at some point in the source code it got renamed to JailT. Cool name. Furthermore, the implementation changed rather dramatically from the blog post, so let’s chase the implementation as given. I’ll reproduce it here:

type RLens r s = Lens s s r r

newtype JailT s r m a =
    JailT
    { runJailT' :: Bool
                -> RLens r s
                -> s
                -> m (a, s, RLens r s, Bool) }
    deriving (Functor, Typeable)

instance (Applicative m, Monad m) => Applicative (JailT s r m) where
    pure x = JailT $ \v l s -> pure (x, s, l, v)
    (<*>)  = ap

instance (Applicative m, Monad m) => Monad (JailT s r m) where
    return   = pure
    ac >>= k = JailT $ \v l s ->
        if v
            then do
                (x, st', l', v') <- runJailT' ac v l s
                runJailT' (k x) v' l' st'
            else return (undefined, s, l, v)

Already there’s a lot to look at. The most immediate thing that strikes me is the formatting; now I’m very much a “use two spaces for indent” kind of guy — Haskell doesn’t provide many opportunities for natural linebreaks, and our horizontal space is much more limited than our vertical space. So don’t throw away your horizontal budget on initial spacing. It’s minor, but being an artisan means caring about the minor details.

newtype JailT s r m a = JailT
  { runJailT'
      :: Bool
      -> RLens r s
      -> s
      -> m (a, s, RLens r s, Bool)
  }
  deriving (Functor, Typeable)

Much nicer.

The other exciting thing to see in the earlier snippet is that this code comes from before the Functor-Applicative-Monad transition. Which is to say that it’s from the long long ago before Applicative was a superclass on Monad. There’s some history for you.

And then there is the elephant in the room. Whatever this Bool is being passed around by runJailT', the Monad instance branches on it and returns undefined when it’s False. What the hell is that???? Digging into the MonadPlus instance provides some insight:

instance (Applicative m, Monad m) => MonadPlus (JailT s r m) where
    mplus x y = JailT $ \v l s -> do
        x'@(xa, xs, xl, v') <- runJailT' x v l s
        if v'
           then return x'
           else runJailT' y v l s
    mzero = JailT $ \v l s -> return (undefined, s, l, False)

So mzero returns undefined and some False value, presumably which is there to try to warn someone that there’s an undefined floating around.

This is a stupid design. If you’re ever in the business of needing to store data-which-might-not-be-valid and a separate tag stating whether or not it’s valid, a much better design here would be to just use Maybe a instead of (a, Bool).

In fact, perhaps I realized this later on, because runJailT does exactly this logic:

runJailT :: (Functor m)
         => JailT s s m a
         -> s
         -> m (Maybe (a, s))
runJailT ac = fmap (\(a, s, _, v) ->
                            if v then Just (a, s) else Nothing)
                    . runJailT' ac True id

Let’s roll back a bit. The pivotal primitive of JailT is the aptly-named jail:

jail :: (Monad m)
     => RLens r' r
     -> JailT s r' m a
     -> JailT s r m a
jail l' m = JailT $ \v l s -> do
    (a, s', _, v') <- runJailT' m v (l . l') s
    return (a, s', l, v')

Pretty reasonable definition here. I’m not sure what the idea behind RLens being a flipped version of Lens' was for. The only odd choice here is that in the big tuple returned in jail, l gets passed along unchanged. We can tell from looking at it that l here is the current lens we’re looking at. But jail is the only primitive that changes the lens, and it takes a JailT as an argument. Which is all to say that there isn’t anything actually stateful going on with the RLens. So without looking any further, I’d bet dollars to donuts that this l getting returned is purely vestigial and serves absolutely no purpose. Which in turn means we should be able to chop it out of the definition of JailT.

Speaking of stupid anti-patterns, here’s another one:

into :: RLens a (Maybe a)
into = lens fromJust (const Just)

jailMaybe :: (Applicative m, Monad m)
          => RLens (Maybe r') r
          -> a
          -> JailT s r' m a
          -> JailT s r m a
jailMaybe l d m =
    (gets $ view l) >>= \case
        Just _  -> jail (l . into) m
        Nothing -> return d

This is horrendous for a few reasons. into is an unsafe lens that will crash if you try to read out of a Nothing. But then that behavior is guarded in jailMaybe by checking that it isn’t already nothing. Stupid.

The last function I want to point out is parole:

parole :: (Applicative m, Monad m)
       => a
       -> JailT s r m (Maybe a)
       -> JailT s r m a
parole d m = do
    this <- get
    m >>= \case
        Just a  -> return a
        Nothing -> put this >> return d

which… does… something. I guess it attempts to run a Maybe-valued JailT, and if it fails, unwinds the state and returns some default a. Rearing its ugly head here, however, is the ghost of the undefined nonsense from mzero. Note that if we invoke parole a mzero we will get a crash rather than the roll-back-and-default behavior that it promises on the tin.

So, all in all, I am not particularly impressed with my first monad. Here’s how I’d write it today.

First, I don’t think I’ve written a “control”-y sort of monad from scratch in the last five years. Whatever behavior you want is almost always just the composition of a few monad transformers. In this case, we have a Reader for the current lens, a State for the original state, and a Maybe to give us mzero semantics.

Since we want our state to roll-back when we take an alternative path, we must put MaybeT underneath our StateT.1 This gives us the nice formulation of a JailT as:

newtype JailT s r m a = JailT
  { unJailT :: ReaderT (ALens' s r) (StateT s (MaybeT m)) a
  }

(we use ALens' s r here instead of Lens' s r since the latter requires -XImpredicativeTypes. Which happens to be turned on in the original implementation!)

Once nice thing about defining our monad as a newtype over a series of monad transformers, is that it allows us to newtype-derive all of the relevant instances:

  deriving newtype (Functor, Applicative, Monad, MonadIO, Alternative)

No implementation for such things is required, and therefore we know that the derived instances must be correct. Which means we have many fewer things to worry about.

I prefer to use unWhatever as my naming scheme for these newtypes, so that I can provide runWhatever as a more user-friendly function.

runJailT :: s -> Lens' s t -> JailT s t m a -> m (Maybe (a, s))
runJailT s l = runMaybeT . flip runStateT s . flip runReaderT l . unJailT

What’s also nice about using standard monad transformers for your implementation is that you can reuse all of their existing combinators. For example, to implement jail all we need to do is invoke withReaderT :: (r' -> r) -> ReaderT r m a -> ReaderT r' m a, which lets us change the type of the reader.

jail :: Lens' t u -> JailT s u m a -> JailT s t m a
jail ltu = JailT . withReaderT (\lst -> cloneLens lst . ltu) . unJailT

Notice here that I like to minimize my points without going point-free; jail as written is very legible, but writing it entirely pointfree is a crime against humanity:

-- don't do this!
jail = (JailT .) . (. unJailT) . withReaderT . flip ((.) . cloneLens)

Rather than implementing parole directly, we can note that it is the composition of two pieces — (1) attempt something, (2) return a default if it failed. Whenever you notice de-composition opportunities like this, take them!

We can write attempt, which is wildly general and doesn’t care one fig about jails or the legal system:

attempt :: (Alternative m, Monad m) => m (Maybe a) -> m a
attempt m = maybe empty pure =<< m

and then parole is merely

parole :: Monad m => a -> JailT s t m (Maybe a) -> JailT s t m a
parole a0 j =
  asum
    [ attempt j
    , pure a0
    ]

All in all, significantly nicer if you ask me. But I’m just a TV. Don’t take my word for it. Compare for yourself!

Original Implementation 
{-# LANGUAGE GeneralizedNewtypeDeriving,
             FlexibleInstances, MultiParamTypeClasses,
             DeriveFunctor, ImpredicativeTypes, LambdaCase,
             DeriveDataTypeable #-}

import Control.Applicative (Alternative(..))
import Control.Monad (ap, MonadPlus(..))
import Control.Monad.State
import Control.Lens
import Data.Maybe (fromJust)
import Data.Typeable


type RLens r s = Lens s s r r

newtype JailT s r m a =
    JailT
    { runJailT' :: Bool
                -> RLens r s
                -> s
                -> m (a, s, RLens r s, Bool) }
    deriving (Functor, Typeable)

instance (Applicative m, Monad m) => Applicative (JailT s r m) where
    pure x = JailT $ \v l s -> pure (x, s, l, v)
    (<*>)  = ap

instance (Applicative m, Monad m) => Monad (JailT s r m) where
    return   = pure
    ac >>= k = JailT $ \v l s ->
        if v
            then do
                (x, st', l', v') <- runJailT' ac v l s
                runJailT' (k x) v' l' st'
            else return (undefined, s, l, v)

instance (Applicative m, Monad m) => MonadState r (JailT s r m) where
    get   = JailT $ \v l s -> return (view l s, s, l, v)
    put x = JailT $ \v l s -> return ((), set l x s, l, v)

instance MonadTrans (JailT s r) where
    lift x = JailT $ \v l s -> x >>= (\a -> return (a, s, l, v))

instance (Applicative m, MonadIO m) => MonadIO (JailT s r m) where
    liftIO = lift . liftIO

instance (Applicative m, Monad m) => MonadPlus (JailT s r m) where
    mplus x y = JailT $ \v l s -> do
        x'@(xa, xs, xl, v') <- runJailT' x v l s
        if v'
           then return x'
           else runJailT' y v l s
    mzero = JailT $ \v l s -> return (undefined, s, l, False)

instance (Applicative m, Monad m) => Alternative (JailT s r m) where
    (<|>) = mplus
    empty = mzero

runJailT :: (Functor m)
         => JailT s s m a
         -> s
         -> m (Maybe (a, s))
runJailT ac = fmap (\(a, s, _, v) ->
                            if v then Just (a, s) else Nothing)
                    . runJailT' ac True id

type Jail s r = JailT s r Identity
runJail :: Jail s s a
        -> s
        -> Maybe (a, s)
runJail ac = runIdentity . runJailT ac

jail :: (Monad m)
     => RLens r' r
     -> JailT s r' m a
     -> JailT s r m a
jail l' m = JailT $ \v l s -> do
    (a, s', _, v') <- runJailT' m v (l . l') s
    return (a, s', l, v')

into :: RLens a (Maybe a)
into = lens fromJust (const Just)

jailMaybe :: (Applicative m, Monad m)
          => RLens (Maybe r') r
          -> a
          -> JailT s r' m a
          -> JailT s r m a
jailMaybe l d m =
    (gets $ view l) >>= \case
        Just _  -> jail (l . into) m
        Nothing -> return d

escape :: (Applicative m, Monad m)
       => JailT s s m a
       -> JailT s r m a
escape m = JailT $ \v l s -> do
    (a, s', _, v') <- runJailT' m v id s
    return (a, s', l, v')

freedom :: (Applicative m, Monad m) => JailT s r m s
freedom = JailT $ \v l s -> return (s, s, l, v)

-- happens to be unused, because it's kinda insane??
overwrite :: (Applicative m, Monad m)
          => RLens r' r
          -> JailT r r' m a
          -> JailT s r m a
overwrite l' m = JailT $ \v l s -> do
    (a, s', _, v') <- runJailT' m v l' $ view l s
    return (a, set l s' s, l, v')

parole :: (Applicative m, Monad m)
       => a
       -> JailT s r m (Maybe a)
       -> JailT s r m a
parole d m = do
    this <- get
    m >>= \case
        Just a  -> return a
        Nothing -> put this >> return d

inspect :: (Applicative m, Monad m)
        => RLens i r
        -> JailT s r m i
inspect l = gets $ view l

inquire :: (Applicative m, Monad m)
        => RLens i s
        -> JailT s r m i
inquire l = view l <$> freedom

arrest :: (Applicative m, Monad m)
       => RLens r' r
       -> r'
       -> JailT s r m ()
arrest l v = do
    state <- get
    put $ set l v state

arrests :: (Applicative m, Monad m)
        => RLens r' r
        -> (r' -> r')
        -> JailT s r m ()
arrests l f = do
    state <- get
    put $ set l (f $ view l state) state

vs the

New Implementation 
{-# LANGUAGE DerivingStrategies         #-}
{-# LANGUAGE FlexibleInstances          #-}
{-# LANGUAGE GeneralizedNewtypeDeriving #-}
{-# LANGUAGE MultiParamTypeClasses      #-}
{-# LANGUAGE RankNTypes                 #-}

import Control.Applicative
import Control.Lens
import Control.Monad.State
import Control.Monad.Reader
import Control.Monad.Trans.Maybe


newtype JailT s r m a = JailT
  { unJailT :: ReaderT (ALens' s r) (StateT s (MaybeT m)) a
  }
  deriving newtype (Functor, Applicative, Monad, MonadIO, Alternative)

instance Monad m => MonadState r (JailT s r m) where
  get = JailT $ do
    l <- asks cloneLens
    gets $ view l
  put r = JailT $ do
    l <- asks cloneLens
    modify $ set l r

runJailT :: s -> Lens' s t -> JailT s t m a -> m (Maybe (a, s))
runJailT s l = runMaybeT . flip runStateT s . flip runReaderT l . unJailT

jail :: Lens' t u -> JailT s u m a -> JailT s t m a
jail ltu = JailT . withReaderT (\lst -> cloneLens lst . ltu) . unJailT

escape :: JailT s s m a -> JailT s t m a
escape (JailT j) = JailT $ withReaderT (const id) j

freedom :: Monad m => JailT s t m s
freedom = JailT get

attempt :: (Alternative m, Monad m) => m (Maybe a) -> m a
attempt m = maybe empty pure =<< m

parole :: Monad m => a -> JailT s t m (Maybe a) -> JailT s t m a
parole a0 j =
  asum
    [ attempt j
    , pure a0
    ]

arrest :: Monad m => Lens' t u -> u -> JailT s t m ()
arrest l u = modify $ set l u

Maybe this was interesting to you. It certainly was fun for me, because I like tearing apart bad code, and I don’t get to see much of it now that I have very talented colleagues. Thankfully I have a huge amount of crap code from my past, including an even more egregious monad that we’ll tackle next time around.

item.title: An Algebraic Theory of Music
item.author: sandy@sandymaguire.me (Sandy Maguire)
item.content:encoded:
In my last post, I was struggling towards an algebraic theory of music. This idea has been burning in my mind ever since, and I wanted to give some updates with where I’ve landed.

Differentiating Voices from Music

We begin by modeling a musical voice, which is, roughly speaking, the abstract version of a human voice. The voice can be doing one thing at a time, or can choose to not be doing anything.

Voices are modeled by step functions, which are divisions of the real line into discrete chunks. We interpret each discrete chunk as a note being played by the voice for the duration of the chunk.

This gives rise to a nice applicative structure that I alluded to in my previous post:

liftA2 f
  |---- a ----|-- b --|
  |-- x --|---- y ----|
=
  |- fax -|fay|- fby -|

where we take the union of the note boundaries in order to form the applicative. If either voice is resting, so too is the applicative. There is also an Alternative instance here, which chooses the first non-rest.

There is a similar monoidal structure here, where multiplication is given by “play these two things simultaneously,” relying on an underlying Semigroup instance for the meaning of “play these two things:”

instance Semigroup a => Semigroup (Voice a)
instance Semigroup a => Monoid (Voice a)

If either voice is resting, we treat its value as mempty, and can happily combine the two parts in parallel.

All of this gives rise to the following rich structure:

newtype Voice a = Voice { unVoice :: SF Time (Maybe a) }
  deriving stock
    (Eq, Ord, Show, Functor, Foldable, Traversable, Generic, Generic1)
  deriving newtype
    (Semigroup, Monoid)
  deriving
    Applicative
    via Compose (SF Time) Maybe

instance Filterable Voice
instance Witherable Voice
instance Alternative Voice

-- | Delay a voice by some amount of time.
delayV :: Time -> Voice a -> Voice a

From Voices to Music

Voices, therefore, give us our primitive notion of monophony. But real music usually has many voices doing many things, independently. This was a point in which I got stuck in my previous post.

The solution here, is surprisingly easy. Assign a Voice to each voice name:

newtype Music v a = Music
  { getVoices :: v -> Voice a
  }
  deriving stock
    (Functor, Generic, Functor)
  deriving newtype
    (Semigroup, Monoid)
  deriving (Applicative, Alternative)
    via Compose ((->) v) Voice

instance Profunctor Music

instance Finite v => Foldable (Music v)
instance Finite v => Traversable (Music v)
instance Filterable (Music v)
instance Finite v => Witherable (Music v)

We get an extremely rich structure here completely for free. Our monoid combines all voices in parallel; our applicative combines voices pointwise; etc. However, we also have a new Profunctor Music instance, whose characteristic lmap :: (b -> c) -> Music c a -> Music b a method allows us to trade lines between voices.

In addition to the in-parallel monoid instance, we can also define a tile product operator over Music v a, which composes things sequentially1:

duration :: Music v a -> Time

(##) :: Semigroup a => Music v a -> Music v a -> Music v a
m@(Music m1) ## Music m2 =
    Music $ liftA2 (<>) m1 $ fmap (delayV $ duration m) m2

The Semigroup a constraint on (##) arises from the fact that the pieces of music might extend off to infinity in either direction (which pure @Voice must do), and we need to deal with that.

There are a few other combinators we care about. First, we can lift anonymous voices (colloquially “tunes”) into multi-part Music:

voice :: Eq v => v -> Music () a -> Music v a
voice v (Music sf) = Music $
  \case
    ((== v) -> True) -> sf ()
    _ -> mempty

and we can assign the same line to everyone:

everyone :: Music () a -> Music v a
everyone (Music m) = Music $ const $ m ()

Writing Lines

The primitives for building little tunes are

note :: Time -> a -> Music () a
rest :: Time -> Music () a

which you can then compose sequentially via (##), and assign to voices via voice.

Harmonic Constraints

One of the better responses to my last blog post was a link to Dmitri Tymoczko’s FARM 2024 talk.

There’s much more in this video than I can possibly due justice to here, but my big takeaway was that this guy is thinking about the same sorts of things that I am. So I dove into his work, and that lead to his quadruple hierarchy:

Voices move within chords, which move within scales, which move within macro-harmonies.

Tymoczko presents a T algebra which is a geometric space for reasoning about voice leadings. He’s got a lot of fun websites for exploring the ideas, but I couldn’t find an actual implementation of the idea anywhere, so I cooked one up myself.

The idea here is that we have some T :: [Nat] -> Type which describes a hierarchy of abstract scales moving with respect to one another. For example, the Western traditional of having triads move within the diatonic scale, which moves within the chromatic scale, would be represented as T '[3, 7, 12]. T forms a monoid, and has some simple generators that give rise to smooth voice leadings (chord changes.)

Having a model for smooth harmonic transformations means we can use it constructively. I am still working out the exact details here, but the rough shape of the idea is to build an underlying field of key changes (represented as smooth voice leadings in T '[7, 12]):

keyChanges :: Music () (T '[7, 12])

We can then make an underlying field of functional harmonic changes (chord changes), modeled as smooth voice leadings in T '[3, 7]:

chordChanges :: Music () (T '[3, 7])

Our voices responsible for harmony can now be written as values of type

harmonicVoices :: Music h (Set (T '[3]))

and we can use the applicative musical structure to combine the elements together:

{-# LANGUAGE ApplicativeDo #-}

extend :: T ns -> T (ns ++ ms)
sink   :: T ns -> T (n ': ns)

harmony :: Music h (Set (T '[3, 7, 12]))
harmony = do
  k <- everyone keyChanges
  c <- everyone chordChanges
  m <- harmonicVoices
  pure $ extend m <> extend c <> sink k

which we can later fmap out into concrete pitches. The result is that we can completely isolate the following pieces:

  • key changes
  • chord changes
  • how voices express the current harmony
  • the rhythms of all of the above

and the result is guaranteed to compose in a way that the ear can interpret as music. Not necessarily good music, but undeniably as music.

The type indices on T are purely for my book-keeping, and nothing requires them to be there. Which means we could also use the applicative structure to modulate over different sorts of harmony (eg, move from triads to seventh chords.)

Melody: Still an Open Question

I haven’t quite gotten a feel for melody yet; I think it’s probably in T '[7, 12], but it would be nice to be able to target chord tones as well. Please let me know in the comments if you have any insight here.

However, I have been thinking about contouring, which is the overall “shape” of a musical line. Does it go up, and peak in the middle, and then come down again? Or maybe it smoothly descends down.

We can use the discrete intervals intrinsic inside of Voices to find “reasonable” times to sample them. In essence this assigns a Time to each segment:

timed :: Music v a -> Music v (Time, a)

and we can then use these times to then sample a function Time -> b. This then allows us to apply contours (given as regular Real -> Real functions) to arbitrary rhythms. I currently have this typed as

contour :: Group a => a -> (Real -> Real) -> Music v () -> Music v a

where a ~ T something, and the outputted Reals get rounded to their nearest integer values. I’m not deeply in love with this type, but the rough idea is great—turn arbitrary real-valued functions into musical lines. This generalizes contouring, as well as scale runs.

Next Steps?

I’m writing all of this up because I go back to work on Monday and life is going to get very busy soon. I’m afraid I won’t be able to finish all of this!

The types above I’m pretty certain are relatively close to perfect. They seem to capture everything I could possibly want, and nothing I don’t want. Assuming I’m right about that, they must make up the basis of musical composition.

The next step therefore is to build musical combinators on top. One particular combinator I’ve got my eye on is some sort of general ~> “get from here to there” operator:

(~>) :: (Semigroup a, ???) => Music v a -> Music v a -> Music v a

which I imagine would bridge a gap between the end of one piece of music with beginning of another. I think this would be roughly as easy as moving each voice linearly in T space from where it was to where it needs to be. This might need to be a ternary operation in order to also associate a rhythmic pattern to use for the bridge.

But I imagine (~>) would be great for lots of dumb little musical things. Like when applied over the chord dimension, it would generate arpeggios. Over the scale dimension, it would generate runs. And it would make chromatic moves in the chroma dimension.

Choosing exactly what moves to make for Ts consisting of components in multiple axes might just be some bespoke order, or could do something more intelligent. I think the right approach would be to steal diagrams’ idea of an Envelope, and attach some relevant metadata to each Music. We could then write (~>) as a function of those envelopes, but I must admit I don’t quite know what this would look like.

As usual, I’d love any insight you have! Please leave it in the comments. Although I must admit I appreciate comments of the form “have you tried $X” much more than of the form “music is sublime and you’re an idiot for even trying this.”

Happy new year!

  1. Strictly speaking, the tile product can also do parallel composition, as well as sychronizing composition, but that’s not super important right now.↩︎
